la:verb:icio.html:
ī^cĭo and ī^co), īci, ictum (forms in use, only
pres. icit, iciunt, icere; perf. icit, icisse; pluperf. iceram, iceras; fut. perf. icero; pass. pres. icitur, icimur; perf. ictus est; and part. ictus, a, um; pres. ĭco, P.; but īcit,; ; pres. icio, ; P.), 3, v. a.
Gr. ἰπ-, ἴπτομαι, to injure; ἴψ, a worm; ἴκρια, scaffolding; cf. Ἴκαρος, ἐν-ιπή
, to strike, hit, smite, stab, sting (cf.: ferio, percutio, verbero, pulso).
Lit. (rare but class.).
In gen.: exim corpus propellit et icit,: unde icimur ictu,: femur,: caput telis (musca),: vidulum fuscinā, Plaut. Fragm. ap. : cum Ptolemaeus in proelio telo venenato ictus esset,; cf.: lapide ictus,: ibi in turba ictus Remus, cecidit,: velut ictus ab Hercule Cacus,.—
Esp. of lightning, etc., to strike: cum Summanus e caelo ictus esset,: ictae limen domus,: fulmine laurus sola non icitur,; cf.: fulmen lauri fruticem non icit,; so in a figure, of a thunderbolt: ut vos iisdem ignibus circumsaepti me primum ictum pro vobis et fumantem videretis,; cf.: exin candida se radiis dedit icta foras lux (i. e. Aurora), struck with rays, irradiated, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 93 Vahl.).—
With a homogeneous object: Icere colaphum, to give a box on the ear: hei, colaphum icit,.—
Trop.
In partic., icere foedus, like ferire and percutere foedus (v. ferio and percutio, I. B. fin.), to make a covenant or league: foedus, quod meo sanguine in pactione provinciarum iceras, frangere noluisti,: cum Gaditanis foedus icisse dicitur,; Cael. ap. P.: orsi a foedere quod nobiscum icerant,—
(Perh. not ante - Aug.) Desideriis icta fidelibus Quaerit patria Caesarem, smitten, tormented, : novā re consules icti,disturbed,; cf. : conscientiā ictus,: metu icta, et saep.: haud secus quam pestifero sidere icti pavebant,panic - stricken,: domestico vulnere ictus,by family affliction,: si existunt, qui magnitudinem multum ultra se positam non icturi appetant,reach, attain,—
Poet.: saltat Milonius, ut semel icto Accessit fervor capiti numerusque lucernis,i. e. smitten with wine, tipsy,.

la:noun:Icarus.html:
Īcărus, i, m., = Ἴκαρος.
A son of Dœdalus, who, on his flight from Crete, fell into the Ægean Sea, ; ; .—
Derivv.
īcărĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Icarus, Icarian: aquae,the part of the Ægean Sea named after Icarus,.—Also absol.: īcărĭum (sc. mare), ; : fluctus,: litus,.—
Icăros, i, f., one of the Sporades, .—
=Ἰκάριος, son of Œbalus, king of Sparta, the father of Erigone and Penelope, placed in the heavens as the constellation Bŏōtes, ; (3, 31), 29; ; .—Called also īcărĭus, ; .—
Derivv.
īcărĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Icarus, Icarian: palmes,i. e. the vine, which Bacchus taught Icarus to cultivate,; cf. umbra,i. e. of the vine,: boves, the constellation Bŏōtes, (3, 31), 24: canis stella, i. e. the constellation Canis Major (the dog of Icarus, named Mæra, which was translated to the sky), ; so, astrum,; hence also: latratus,.—
īcăris, ĭdis, = Ἰκαρίς, the daughter of Icarus, i. e. Penelope, .—
īcărĭōtis, ĭdis, f., = Ἰκαριωτίς, the daughter of Icarus, i. e. Penelope, (4, 12), 10.—Adj.: tela,i. e. of Penelope,.

la:noun:ichneumon.html:
ichneumon, ŏnis, m., = ἰχνεύμων.
An animal which tracks the crocodile and destroys its eggs; the Egyptian rat or ichneumon, ; sq.; ; ; .—
An insect, the ichneumon-fly, Sphex sabulosus, Linn.; ; .
